doc.title: Dave Bennett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 16, 2025

title: Learning by ear, the Clarkston jam sessions and Tad Weed on chords
summary: He learned from records, a teacher Jamie McLeod and old-timer jams at 13, only grasping chords in his twenties from Tad Weed; now he is brushing up on reading.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: That’s saying a lot. Was there a point where you started to realize, you know you’re learning these improvisations by ear? When did you connect to keys and form and relate what he was playing to chords?

Chords came much later. But as far as knowing keys and form when I was 13 my dad saw an ad in the local paper and it said the Clarkston — Clarkston is a town right near where I live here. I live in Waterford, Michigan. And it said that the Clarkston Senior Center, they were having, every Tuesday, a jam session for anybody that wanted to come to play, one until four. So he took me over there and there was a group of old timers that would get together and jam every Tuesday. And I joined them every week. So when they would say let’s do, I don’t know, “Sentimental Journey” in the key of C. Well I didn’t understand what that meant but then I figured it out for myself that, relative from concert pitch to B flat and I thought oh, okay, so that’s what that means. So I would just listen very carefully and try to figure that out. Chords, that didn’t really make much sense to me until probably my early twenties. I had a friend of mine that played piano for me, Tad Weed, who was an amazing jazz teacher too. So at that point I could play all these things by ear, I just didn’t know what I was doing, really. And so I’d come to him and say, “What is this and why does it sound this way?” And he was able to go to the piano and show me and explain diminished, augmented, why I would play a certain run over a chord and why it sounded that way. And so I did things a bit in reverse. You know I could hear these things and play them I just didn’t quite know what I was doing. So like you know right now I’m trying to get my reading back and my theory back, so I’ve been doing a deep dive into that. It tends to go away pretty quickly if you don’t stay on top.
I know what you mean. It’s surprising after like oh my God it’s been like twelve months since I actually sat in an ensemble and read a chart.

Exactly. Yeah. So I’m guesting with a big band on Tuesday and we’re doing three Gordon Goodwin charts, okay? And I haven’t sat down to read a piece of music in quite a while so they handed me the charts and I looked at it and I thought yeah, I better start brushing up on this. So those have been my days and nights here.
I love that phrase, because I’ve heard it from other interviewees, in that “I didn’t really know what I was doing.” In effect you did because your ear was telling you that it’s okay.
And sometimes if you learn about these things beforehand they seem imposing. And I’m not sure I want to go there. So maybe playing by ear has a benefit to it.

Probably. I mean it helped me you know. I mean even now I can look at a piece of music and it seems overwhelming when you see all the — what’s there. But then once you play it I’m thinking oh, maybe it’s not so bad after all. So maybe it’s just getting past some of that fear and that overwhelming feeling you know. At least for me.
